nodes.name: $k$--coloring
nodes.statement: A \emph{$k$--coloring} of a set $X$ is a map $c:X\rightarrow [k]$ where $[k]=\{1,2,...k\}$.

nodes.name: rainbow subset
nodes.statement: A subset $Y\subset X$ is {\em rainbow} under $c$ if the coloring assigns pairwise distinct colors to the elements of $Y$.
differentia: the coloring assigns pairwise distinct colors to the elements of $Y$

nodes.name: The prime classes ${\mathcal P}_0$ and ${\mathcal P}_1$
nodes.statement: We denote by ${\mathcal P}_0$ the set of primes $p$ for which $2$ has either multiplicative order $p-1$, or multiplicative order $(p-1)/2$ with $(p-1)/2$ odd. Let ${\mathcal P}_1$ be the set of remaining primes.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{P}_0$ collects primes $p$ where $2$ has order $p-1$ or odd order $(p-1)/2$; $\mathcal{P}_1$ is the rest.
differentia: $2$ has either multiplicative order $p-1$, or multiplicative order $(p-1)/2$ with $(p-1)/2$ odd

nodes.name: $m(n)$
nodes.statement: Following \cite{jungic} we let $m(n)$ denote the largest integer $m$ for which there is a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $\Z/n\Z$ such that the cardinality of the smallest color class is $m$.
nodes.origin_citation: Jungi\'c, Licht, Mahdian, Ne\v set\v ril, Radoi\v ci\'c 2003
nodes.statement_short: $m(n)$ is the largest possible size of the smallest color class of a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
differentia: there is a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $\Z/n\Z$ such that the cardinality of the smallest color class is $m$

nodes.name: Minkowski sum
nodes.statement: Recall that the Minkowski sum of two nonempty subsets $X,Y\subset G$ is defined as $$ X+Y=\{ x+y: x\in X, y\in Y\}. $$
differentia: X+Y=\{ x+y: x\in X, y\in Y\}

nodes.name: period (stabilizer) $P(S)$
nodes.statement: The \emph{period} (or stabilizer) of a subset $S\subseteq G$, denoted by $P (S)$, is the subgroup of $G$ defined by:} $$P (S)=\{g\in G:S+g=S\}$$

nodes.name: $H$--periodic, periodic, aperiodic set
nodes.statement: We say that a set $S$ is $H$--{\it periodic}, where $H$ is a subgroup of $G$, if $S+H=S$, and $S$ is {\em periodic} if $P(S)$ is a nontrivial subgroup of $G$ (i.e. $P(S)\neq \{0\}$). \textcolor{black}{ If $P(S)=\{ 0\}$ we say that $S$ is {\it aperiodic}.
nodes.statement_short: A set is $H$--periodic if it is invariant under translation by $H$, periodic if its period is nontrivial, aperiodic otherwise.

nodes.name: rainbow--free $3$--coloring
nodes.statement: A $3$--term arithmetic progression is an ordered triple $(x,y,z)$ with $x,y,z\in G$ satisfying the equation $x+y=2z$. In the present setting we say that a $3$--coloring of the elements of $G$ is \emph{rainbow--free} if there are no rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progressions.
nodes.statement_short: A $3$--coloring of $G$ is rainbow--free when no triple $(x,y,z)$ with $x+y=2z$ gets three distinct colors.
differentia: there are no rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progressions

nodes.name: $H$--quasiperiodic set
nodes.statement: A set $S\subset G$ is said to be $H$--{\em quasiperiodic} if it admits a decomposition $S=S_0\cup S_1$, where each of $S_0$ and $S_1$ can be empty, $S_1$ is a maximal $H$--periodic subset of $S$ and $S_0$ is (properly) contained in a single coset of $H$. Note that every set $S\subset G$ is quasiperiodic with $S_1=\emptyset$ and $H=G$.
nodes.statement_short: $S$ is $H$--quasiperiodic if it splits as a maximal $H$--periodic part plus a piece inside one $H$--coset.
differentia: it admits a decomposition $S=S_0\cup S_1$, where each of $S_0$ and $S_1$ can be empty, $S_1$ is a maximal $H$--periodic subset of $S$ and $S_0$ is (properly) contained in a single coset of $H$

nodes.name: triple of $H$--cosets in arithmetic progression
nodes.statement: We say that a triple $( X,Y,Z)$ of $H$--cosets is in arithmetic progression if $(X/H)+(Y/H)=2\cdot (Z/H)$. For $X$ an $H$--coset and $U$ a color class of a coloring we write $X_U:=X\cap U$.

nodes.name: $H$--regular coloring
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{The coloring is said to be $H$--{\it regular} if, up to transllation, it satisfies conditions (i), (ii) and (iii) of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} for the subgroup $H<G$.}
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion
nodes.statement_short: A coloring is $H$--regular when, up to translation, it satisfies conditions (i)--(iii) of the main theorem for $H$.
differentia: it satisfies conditions (i), (ii) and (iii) of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} for the subgroup $H<G$

nodes.name: almost--progression
nodes.statement: An {\it almost}--progression is an arithmetic progression with one point removed. Observe that, with this definition, the class of almost progressions contains the class of all arithmetic progressions except the ones whose length equals the order of the cyclic group generated by the difference.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: almost $H$--quasiperiodic set
nodes.statement: A set $X\subset G$ is {\it almost} $H$--quasiperiodic (resp. almost $H$--periodic) if there is $x\in G$ such that $X\cup \{ x\}$ is $H$--quasiperiodic (resp. $H$--periodic).
differentia: there is $x\in G$ such that $X\cup \{ x\}$ is $H$--quasiperiodic (resp. $H$--periodic)

nodes.name: punctured coset
nodes.statement: We say that a coset $X$ of a subgroup $H<G$ is punctured if all but one of its elements are in the same color class $U\in \{ A,B,C\}$. We then say that $X$ is a punctured coset of color $U$.
differentia: all but one of its elements are in the same color class $U\in \{ A,B,C\}$

nodes.name: Jungi\'c et al. characterization of $n$ admitting rainbow--free $3$--colorings
nodes.statement: For every integer $n$, there is a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $\Z/n\Z$ with non--empty color classes, if and only if $n$ does not satisfy any of the following conditions: \textcolor{black}{ \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $n$ is a power of $2$. \item[(b)] $n$ is a prime and the multiplicative order of $2$ is $n-1$. \item[(b)] $n$ is a prime, the multiplicative order of $2$ is $(n-1)/2$ and $(n-1)/2$ is odd. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Jungi\'c, Licht, Mahdian, Ne\v set\v ril, Radoi\v ci\'c 2003
nodes.statement_short: $\Z/n\Z$ has a rainbow--free $3$--coloring with non-empty classes iff $n$ is not a power of $2$ and not one of two exceptional prime types.
assumptions: For every integer $n$
conclusions: there is a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $\Z/n\Z$ with non--empty color classes, if and only if $n$ does not satisfy any of the following conditions:
$n$ is a power of $2$.
$n$ is a prime and the multiplicative order of $2$ is $n-1$.
$n$ is a prime, the multiplicative order of $2$ is $(n-1)/2$ and $(n-1)/2$ is odd.

nodes.name: Jungi\'c et al. bounds on $m(n)$
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be not a power of $2$, $q$ be the smallest prime factor of $n$, and $r$ be the smallest odd prime factor of $n$, then: $$\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2r} \right\rfloor \le m(n) \le min (\frac{n}{6}, \frac{n}{q})$$
nodes.origin_citation: Jungi\'c, Licht, Mahdian, Ne\v set\v ril, Radoi\v ci\'c 2003
nodes.statement_short: $m(n)$ is squeezed between $\lfloor n/2r\rfloor$ and $\min(n/6, n/q)$ for $q,r$ the smallest (odd) prime factors.
assumptions: Let $n$ be not a power of $2$
$q$ be the smallest prime factor of $n$
$r$ be the smallest odd prime factor of $n$
conclusions: $$\left\lfloor \frac{n}{2r} \right\rfloor \le m(n) \le min (\frac{n}{6}, \frac{n}{q})$$

nodes.name: Conjecture of Jungi\'c, Ne\v set\v ril and Radoi\v ci\'c on $m(n)$
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be an integer which is not a power of $2$. Let $p$ denote the smallest odd prime factor of $n$ in ${\mathcal P}_0$ and let $q$ be the smallest odd prime factor of $n$ in ${\mathcal P}_1$. Then the largest cardinality of the smallest color class in a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of the cyclic group $\Z/n\Z$ satisfies $$m(n)=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{\min \{2p,q\}}\right\rfloor.$$
nodes.origin_citation: Jungi\'c, Ne\v set\v ril, Radoi\v ci\'c 2005
nodes.statement_short: Conjecturally $m(n)=\lfloor n/\min\{2p,q\}\rfloor$, with $p\in\mathcal{P}_0$, $q\in\mathcal{P}_1$ the smallest odd prime factors.
assumptions: Let $n$ be an integer which is not a power of $2$.
Let $p$ denote the smallest odd prime factor of $n$ in ${\mathcal P}_0$
let $q$ be the smallest odd prime factor of $n$ in ${\mathcal P}_1$
conclusions: the largest cardinality of the smallest color class in a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of the cyclic group $\Z/n\Z$ satisfies
$$m(n)=\left\lfloor \frac{n}{\min \{2p,q\}}\right\rfloor.$$

nodes.name: Computing the exact value of $m(n)$
nodes.statement: ``Computing the exact value of $m(n)$ remains a challenge''
nodes.origin_citation: Jungi\'c, Ne\v set\v ril, Radoi\v ci\'c 2005
nodes.statement_short: Determining $m(n)$ exactly is stated as an open challenge.

nodes.name: Counterexample to Conjecture for abelian groups of even order
nodes.statement: Let \textcolor{black}{$G:=H\oplus (\Z/2\Z\oplus \Z/2\Z)$} where $|H|$ is not a power of $2$. Consider the following $3$--coloring of $G$: let the subgroup $H$ be colored by $A$, color one of the three remaining $H$--cosets of $G$ by $B$ and the two cosets left by $C$. This coloring |textcolor{black}{has no rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progressions, since such a progression (a triple $(x,y,z)$ such that $x-2y+z=0$) must have two of its elements in the same $H$--coset.} However the smaller color class has cardinality $|H|= |G|/4$ which can be arbitrarily larger than $\min \{\frac{|G|}{2p},\frac{|G|}{q}\}$ according to the choice of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Colouring $H\oplus(\Z/2\Z)^2$ by cosets of $H$ is rainbow--free with smallest class $|G|/4$, breaking the conjecture in the even non-cyclic case.

nodes.name: Translation invariance of rainbow--freeness
nodes.statement: Note that the property of being rainbow--free is invariant by translations: $c$ is a rainbow--free coloring of $G$ if and only if, for each fixed $g\in G$, the coloring $c'(x):=c(x+g)$ is also rainbow--free. We will often use this remark without explicit reference.
nodes.statement_short: Rainbow--freeness is preserved under translating the coloring.

nodes.name: Theorem (main structural characterization of rainbow--free $3$--colorings)
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order $n$ and let $c$ be a $3$--coloring of $G$ with non--empty color classes $A,B,C$. Then $c$ is rainbow--free if and only if, up to translation, there is a proper subgroup $H<G$ and a color class, say $A$, such that \textcolor{black}{the following three conditions hold:} \begin{enumerate} \item[{\rm (i)}] $A\subseteq H$, and the $3$--coloring induced in $H$ is rainbow--free, \item[{\rm (ii)}] \textcolor{black}{both $\widetilde{B}=B\setminus H$ and $\widetilde{C}=C\setminus H$ are $H$--periodic sets, and} \item[{\rm (iii)}] $\widetilde{B}=-\widetilde{B}=2\cdot\widetilde{B}$ and $\widetilde{C}=-\widetilde{C}=2\cdot\widetilde{C}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A $3$--coloring of an odd-order abelian group is rainbow--free exactly when one class sits in a proper subgroup $H$ and the other two are $H$--periodic, symmetric and doubling-invariant outside $H$.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a finite abelian group of odd order $n$
let $c$ be a $3$--coloring of $G$ with non--empty color classes $A,B,C$
conclusions: c$ is rainbow--free if and only if, up to translation, there is a proper subgroup $H<G$ and a color class, say $A$, such that
$A\subseteq H$, and the $3$--coloring induced in $H$ is rainbow--free
both $\widetilde{B}=B\setminus H$ and $\widetilde{C}=C\setminus H$ are $H$--periodic sets
$\widetilde{B}=-\widetilde{B}=2\cdot\widetilde{B}$ and $\widetilde{C}=-\widetilde{C}=2\cdot\widetilde{C}$.

nodes.name: Kneser's Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $(A,B)$ be a pair of finite non-empty subsets of an abelian group $G$. Then, letting $H:=P(A+B)$, we have: $$|A+B|\ge |A+H|+|B+H|-|H|.$$ Moreover, if $|A+B|\le |A|+|B|-1$ then we have equality.
nodes.statement_short: A sumset is at least as large as the sum of the $H$--saturations minus $|H|$, with equality in the small-doubling regime.
assumptions: Let $(A,B)$ be a pair of finite non-empty subsets of an abelian group $G$
letting $H:=P(A+B)$
conclusions: if $|A+B|\le |A|+|B|-1$ then we have equality

nodes.name: Dichotomy from Kneser's Theorem
nodes.statement: It follows from Kneser`s Theorem that, if $|A+B|\leq|A|+|B|-1$, then either $A+B$ is periodic or $|A+B|=|A|+|B|-1$. We shall use this remark in the following sections.
nodes.statement_short: If $|A+B|\le|A|+|B|-1$ then $A+B$ is either periodic or of size exactly $|A|+|B|-1$.
conclusions: either $A+B$ is periodic or $|A+B|=|A|+|B|-1$

nodes.name: Kemperman Structure Theorem (simplified version)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty subsets of an abelian group $G$ verifying $$|A+B|=|A|+|B|-1\textcolor{black}{\le |G|-2}.$$ If $A+B$ is aperiodic then one of the following holds: \begin{enumerate} \item[{\rm (i)}] $\min\{ |A|,|B|\}=1$. \item[{\rm (ii)}] Both $A$ and $B$ are arithmetic progressions with the same common difference. \item[{\rm (iii)}] Both $A$ and $B$ are $H$--quasiperiodic for some nontrivial proper subgroup $H<G$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Grynkiewicz's extension of KST (simplified version)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty subsets of an abelian group $G$ of odd order $n$ verifying $$|A+B|=|A|+|B|\le |G|-3.$$ If $A+B$ is aperiodic then one of the following holds: \begin{enumerate} \item[{\rm (i)}] $\min\{|A|,|B|\}=2$ or $|A|=|B|=3$. \item[{\rm (ii)}] Both $A$ and $B$ are $H$--quasiperiodic for some nontrivial proper subgroup $H<G$. \item[{\rm (iii)}]There are $a, b\in G$ such that $|A'+B'|=|A'|+|B'|-1$ where $A'=A\cup \{ a\}$ and $B'=B\cup \{ b\}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Lemma on $|A|+|B|\ge|G|$
nodes.statement: Let $A,B$ be subsets of a finite abelian group $G$. \textcolor{black}{ \begin{enumerate} \item[{\rm (i)}] If $|A|+|B|>|G|$ then $A+B=G$. \item[{\rm (ii)}] If $|A|+|B|=|G|$ then either $A+B=G$ or there is a subgroup $H$ and $a\in G$ such that both $A$ and $B$ are $H$--periodic and $$A+B=G\setminus (a+H).$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: If $|A|+|B|>|G|$ then $A+B=G$; if $|A|+|B|=|G|$ and $A+B\ne G$ then $A,B$ are $H$--periodic and $A+B$ misses exactly one $H$--coset.

If $|A|+|B|=|G|$ then either $A+B=G$ or there is a subgroup $H$ and $a\in G$ such that both $A$ and $B$ are $H$--periodic and
$$A+B=G\setminus (a+H).$$

nodes.name: The $3$-cosets Lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\{ A,B,C\}$ be a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of an abelian group $G$ with odd order $n$. Let $H<G$ be a subgroup of $G$ and let $(X,Y,Z)$ be a triple of $H$--cosets in arithmetic progression. If each of $X_A$, $Y_B$ and $Z_C$ is non--empty, then \begin{equation} \max\{ |X_A|+|Y_B|, |X_A|+|Z_C|,|Z_C|+|Y_B|\}\leq |H|. \end{equation} \textcolor{black}{In particular, none of the three cosets can be monochromatic.} Moreover, if equality holds then there is a proper subgroup $K<H$ such that two of the sets $X_A, Y_B, Z_C$ are $K$--periodic (the two involved in the equality holding) and the third one is contained in a single coset of $K$.
nodes.statement_short: For three $H$--cosets in arithmetic progression meeting the three colors, pairwise color-intersection sizes sum to at most $|H|$, with a rigid structure in the equality case.

nodes.name: Proposition (the prime case)
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{Let $G$ be a group of prime order $p$ and let $c$ be a $3$--coloring of $G$ with nonempty color classes $A,B,C$. Then $c$ is rainbow--free if and only if, $p\in {\mathcal P}_1$ and, up to translation, there is a color class, say $A$, such that:} \begin{enumerate} \item[{\rm (i)}] \textcolor{black}{$A=\{0\}$,} \item[{\rm (ii)}] \textcolor{black}{$2\cdot B=B=-B$ and $2\cdot C=C=-C$.} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $|G|=p$ prime, rainbow--free $3$--colorings exist exactly when $p\in\mathcal{P}_1$, with one class $\{0\}$ and the others closed under negation and doubling.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a group of prime order $p$ and let $c$ be a $3$--coloring of $G$ with nonempty color classes $A,B,C$.

nodes.name: Corollary (Conjecture holds for abelian groups of odd order)
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be an abelian group of odd order $n$. Let $p$ denote the smallest prime factor of $n$ in ${\mathcal P}_0$ and let $q$ be the smallest prime factor of $n$ in ${\mathcal P}_1$. If $\{A,B,C\}$ is a rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $G$ then \begin{equation}\min\{|A|,|B|,|C|\}\leq \left\lfloor \frac{n}{\min \{2p,q\}}\right\rfloor.\end{equation} Moreover, there are rainbow--free $3$--colorings of $G$ for which equality holds.

nodes.name: Lemma (existence of $K$ with $B+C\supseteq G\setminus K$)

There is a proper subgroup $K$ of $G$ containing $H$ such that $$ B+C\supseteq G\setminus K $$ and each of $B\setminus K$ and $C\setminus K$ is $K$--periodic.

nodes.name: Theorem (structure for cyclic groups of even order)
nodes.statement: Let $G=L\oplus \Z/2^m\Z$ where $L$ has odd order and $m\ge 0$. There is a proper subgroup $H'$ of $L$ such that one of the colors, say $A$, is contained in one coset of $H=H'\oplus \Z/2^m\Z$ and each of $B\setminus H$ and $C\setminus H$ is $H$--periodic.

nodes.name: Proof of the Lemma on $|A|+|B|\ge|G|$
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{We only prove (ii).} If $|A+B|=|G|-1$ then the statement holds with $H=\{ 0\}$. Suppose that $|A+B|\le |G|-2$ and let $H=P(A+B)$ \textcolor{black}{be the period of $A+B$}. By Kneser's Theorem $$|G|>|A+B|=|A+H|+|B+H|-|H|\ge |A|+|B|-|H|=|G|-|H|.$$ \textcolor{black}{Since $A+B$ is $H$--periodic, equality holds in the second inequality.} It follows that $A+B=G\setminus (a+H)$ for some $a\in G$ and that $A+H=A$ and $B+H=B$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Kneser's theorem to the period $H=P(A+B)$ and squeeze the resulting inequalities.

nodes.name: Trivial case $|A+B|=|G|-1$
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{We only prove (ii).} If $|A+B|=|G|-1$ then the statement holds with $H=\{ 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $H=\{0\}$ when the sumset misses a single element.

nodes.name: Case $|A+B|\le|G|-2$ via Kneser
nodes.statement: Suppose that $|A+B|\le |G|-2$ and let $H=P(A+B)$ \textcolor{black}{be the period of $A+B$}. By Kneser's Theorem $$|G|>|A+B|=|A+H|+|B+H|-|H|\ge |A|+|B|-|H|=|G|-|H|.$$ \textcolor{black}{Since $A+B$ is $H$--periodic, equality holds in the second inequality.} It follows that $A+B=G\setminus (a+H)$ for some $a\in G$ and that $A+H=A$ and $B+H=B$.
nodes.statement_short: Kneser's inequality forces equality, so $A+B$ omits exactly one $H$--coset and $A,B$ are $H$--periodic.

nodes.name: Proof of the $3$-cosets Lemma
nodes.statement: Since the coloring is rainbow--free \textcolor{black}{and the three cosets are in arithmetic progression} we have $$X_A+Y_B\subseteq (2\cdot Z)\setminus (2\cdot Z_C).$$ Hence $|X_A+Y_B|<|H|$ which, \textcolor{black}{by Lemma \ref{lem:ph} (i)}, implies $|X_A|+|Y_B|\leq |H|$. Similarly $X_A-(2\cdot Z_C)\varsubsetneq \textcolor{black}{-Y}$ and $Y_B-(2\cdot Z_C)\varsubsetneq \textcolor{black}{-X}$ imply $|X_A|+|Z_C|\le |H|$ and $|Y_B|+|Z_C|\le |H|$ respectively. This proves the first part of the statement. Suppose that $|X_A|+|Y_B|=|H|$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:ph} \textcolor{black}{(ii)} there is a subgroup $K<H$ such that both $X_A$ and $Y_B$ are $K$--periodic and $(2\cdot Z)\setminus (X_A+Y_B)$ consists of a single $K$--coset, which contains $2\cdot Z_C$. A symmetric argument applies if $|X_A|+|Z_C|=|H|$ or $|Y_B|+|Z_C|=|H|$.
nodes.statement_short: Rainbow--freeness confines $X_A+Y_B$ to a proper subset of a coset, then Lemma on $|A|+|B|\ge|G|$ gives the bound and the equality structure.

nodes.name: Derive the three inequalities
nodes.statement: Since the coloring is rainbow--free \textcolor{black}{and the three cosets are in arithmetic progression} we have $$X_A+Y_B\subseteq (2\cdot Z)\setminus (2\cdot Z_C).$$ Hence $|X_A+Y_B|<|H|$ which, \textcolor{black}{by Lemma \ref{lem:ph} (i)}, implies $|X_A|+|Y_B|\leq |H|$. Similarly $X_A-(2\cdot Z_C)\varsubsetneq \textcolor{black}{-Y}$ and $Y_B-(2\cdot Z_C)\varsubsetneq \textcolor{black}{-X}$ imply $|X_A|+|Z_C|\le |H|$ and $|Y_B|+|Z_C|\le |H|$ respectively. This proves the first part of the statement.
nodes.statement_short: Bound each pair of color intersections by $|H|$ using the sumset lemma.

nodes.name: Equality case
nodes.statement: Suppose that $|X_A|+|Y_B|=|H|$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:ph} \textcolor{black}{(ii)} there is a subgroup $K<H$ such that both $X_A$ and $Y_B$ are $K$--periodic and $(2\cdot Z)\setminus (X_A+Y_B)$ consists of a single $K$--coset, which contains $2\cdot Z_C$. A symmetric argument applies if $|X_A|+|Z_C|=|H|$ or $|Y_B|+|Z_C|=|H|$.
nodes.statement_short: In the equality case Lemma (ii) yields the subgroup $K$ and the periodicity structure.

nodes.name: Proof of the Proposition (prime case)
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{Suppose first that $c$ is rainbow--free. Since $G\simeq \Z/p\Z$,} it follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:n/q} that $m(p)\leq 1$ and, from Theorem~\ref{thm:m=0}, that if $p\in {\mathcal P}_0$ then there are no rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $\Z/p\Z$ with non--empty color classes. That is, if $c$ is a rainbow--free $3$--coloring with nonempty color classes, then necessarily $p\in {\mathcal P}_1$ and there is a color class, say $A$, such that $|A|=1$. We can assume that $A=\{0\}$ satisfying (i). To prove (ii) note that, for every $x\in B$, since $G$ is a cyclic group of prime order, then both $-x,2x \in \{B,C\}$. Hence we must have $-x, 2x\in B$, otherwise we get a rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progression of the form $(-x,0,x)$ or $(0,x,2x)$. Thus $2\cdot B=B=-B$ and similarly $2\cdot C=C=-C$. Reciprocally, if the coloring satisfies (i) and (ii), then any $3$--term arithmetic progression containing $0$ has its remaining members in the same color class, thus $c$ is rainbow--free.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions: the cited theorems force a singleton class, and closure under $x\mapsto -x,2x$ then characterizes rainbow--freeness.

nodes.name: Necessity of $p\in\mathcal{P}_1$ and $|A|=1$
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{Suppose first that $c$ is rainbow--free. Since $G\simeq \Z/p\Z$,} it follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:n/q} that $m(p)\leq 1$ and, from Theorem~\ref{thm:m=0}, that if $p\in {\mathcal P}_0$ then there are no rainbow--free $3$--coloring of $\Z/p\Z$ with non--empty color classes. That is, if $c$ is a rainbow--free $3$--coloring with nonempty color classes, then necessarily $p\in {\mathcal P}_1$ and there is a color class, say $A$, such that $|A|=1$. We can assume that $A=\{0\}$ satisfying (i).
nodes.statement_short: Cited bounds on $m(p)$ and the characterization force a singleton color class with $p\in\mathcal{P}_1$.

nodes.name: Closure of $B$ and $C$ under negation and doubling
nodes.statement: To prove (ii) note that, for every $x\in B$, since $G$ is a cyclic group of prime order, then both $-x,2x \in \{B,C\}$. Hence we must have $-x, 2x\in B$, otherwise we get a rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progression of the form $(-x,0,x)$ or $(0,x,2x)$. Thus $2\cdot B=B=-B$ and similarly $2\cdot C=C=-C$.
nodes.statement_short: Avoiding the rainbow triples $(-x,0,x)$ and $(0,x,2x)$ gives $2\cdot B=B=-B$.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Reciprocally, if the coloring satisfies (i) and (ii), then any $3$--term arithmetic progression containing $0$ has its remaining members in the same color class, thus $c$ is rainbow--free.
nodes.statement_short: Conversely (i)+(ii) make every progression through $0$ two-colored.

nodes.name: Proof of the Lemma ($|A|=1$)
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{We may assume that $A=\{0\}$. By choosing $H=\{0\}$, parts (i) and (ii) of Theorem \ref{thm:main} are satisfied.} To prove (iii) note that,\textcolor{black}{ since $G$ is a group of odd order,} for every $x\in B$ then both $-x,2x \in \{B,C\}$. Hence we must have $-x, 2x\in B$, otherwise we get a rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progression of the form $(-x,0,x)$ or $(0,x,2x)$. Thus $2\cdot B=B=-B$ and similarly $2\cdot C=C=-C$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $H=\{0\}$; rainbow-freeness of the triples $(-x,0,x)$ and $(0,x,2x)$ gives condition (iii).

nodes.name: Choose $H=\{0\}$
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{We may assume that $A=\{0\}$. By choosing $H=\{0\}$, parts (i) and (ii) of Theorem \ref{thm:main} are satisfied.}
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (i) and (ii) are immediate for the trivial subgroup.

nodes.name: Verify condition (iii)
nodes.statement: To prove (iii) note that,\textcolor{black}{ since $G$ is a group of odd order,} for every $x\in B$ then both $-x,2x \in \{B,C\}$. Hence we must have $-x, 2x\in B$, otherwise we get a rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progression of the form $(-x,0,x)$ or $(0,x,2x)$. Thus $2\cdot B=B=-B$ and similarly $2\cdot C=C=-C$.
nodes.statement_short: Rainbow-freeness of $(-x,0,x)$ and $(0,x,2x)$ forces $B$ and $C$ closed under negation and doubling.

nodes.name: Proof of the Lemma (one color class inside a single coset)
nodes.statement: We may assume that \textcolor{black}{$0\in A$. Let $H$ be the the minimal proper subgroup of $G$ which contains $A$. } Suppose that $Y\neq H$ is an $H$--coset which intersects the two remaining color classes $B$ and $C$. Let $Z$ be a third coset such that $(X=H,Y,Z)$ are in arithmetic progression. Since $A$ does not meet $Y$ and $Z$, we have $$|Y_B|+|Y_C|+|Z_B|+|Z_C|=2|H|.$$ It follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:3cosets} that $|Y_B|+|Z_C|= |H|$ and $|Y_C|+|Z_B|= |H|$. Moreover, there is a subgroup $K\le H$ such that $X_A=A$ is contained in a single coset of $K$ and each of $Y_B, Y_C,Z_B,Z_C$ is $K$--periodic. By the minimality of $H$ we have $K=H$ contradicting the existence of the bichromatic coset $Y$. \textcolor{black}{Thus parts (i) and (ii) of Theorem \ref{thm:main} are satisfied.} \textcolor{black}{Now consider the $3$--coloring of $G/H$ with color classes $A'=\{ 0\}$, $B'=\widetilde{B}/H$ and $ C'=\widetilde{C}/H$ where $\widetilde{B}=B\setminus H$ and $\widetilde{C}=C\setminus H$. Note that, since the original coloring $\{A,B,C\}$ of $G$ is rainbow--free, then so it is $\{A',B',C'\}$ in $G/H$.} \textcolor{black}{If some of $B'$ or $C'$ is an empty set, then part (iii) of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is clearly satisfied.} \textcolor{black}{If both $B'$ and $C'$ are nonempty sets, then $\{A',B',C'\}$ is a rainbow--free coloring of $G/H$ with nonempty color classes and $|A'|=1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:A=1}}, it follows that $2\cdot B'=B'=-B'$ and $2\cdot C'=C'=-C'$. Thus part (iii) is also satisfied for the coloring $\{A,B,C\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimality of the subgroup containing $A$ rules out bichromatic cosets; then push the coloring to $G/H$ and apply the $|A|=1$ lemma.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: No bichromatic coset by minimality of $H$
nodes.statement: We may assume that \textcolor{black}{$0\in A$. Let $H$ be the the minimal proper subgroup of $G$ which contains $A$. } Suppose that $Y\neq H$ is an $H$--coset which intersects the two remaining color classes $B$ and $C$. Let $Z$ be a third coset such that $(X=H,Y,Z)$ are in arithmetic progression. Since $A$ does not meet $Y$ and $Z$, we have $$|Y_B|+|Y_C|+|Z_B|+|Z_C|=2|H|.$$ It follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:3cosets} that $|Y_B|+|Z_C|= |H|$ and $|Y_C|+|Z_B|= |H|$. Moreover, there is a subgroup $K\le H$ such that $X_A=A$ is contained in a single coset of $K$ and each of $Y_B, Y_C,Z_B,Z_C$ is $K$--periodic. By the minimality of $H$ we have $K=H$ contradicting the existence of the bichromatic coset $Y$. \textcolor{black}{Thus parts (i) and (ii) of Theorem \ref{thm:main} are satisfied.}
nodes.statement_short: A bichromatic coset would contradict minimality of $H$ via the $3$-cosets Lemma.

nodes.name: Induced coloring of $G/H$
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{Now consider the $3$--coloring of $G/H$ with color classes $A'=\{ 0\}$, $B'=\widetilde{B}/H$ and $ C'=\widetilde{C}/H$ where $\widetilde{B}=B\setminus H$ and $\widetilde{C}=C\setminus H$. Note that, since the original coloring $\{A,B,C\}$ of $G$ is rainbow--free, then so it is $\{A',B',C'\}$ in $G/H$.}
nodes.statement_short: Project to $G/H$ with $A'=\{0\}$; the projected coloring stays rainbow--free.

nodes.name: Degenerate case $B'$ or $C'$ empty
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{If some of $B'$ or $C'$ is an empty set, then part (iii) of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is clearly satisfied.}
nodes.statement_short: If one projected class is empty condition (iii) is vacuous.

nodes.name: Both $B'$, $C'$ nonempty
nodes.statement: \textcolor{black}{If both $B'$ and $C'$ are nonempty sets, then $\{A',B',C'\}$ is a rainbow--free coloring of $G/H$ with nonempty color classes and $|A'|=1$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:A=1}}, it follows that $2\cdot B'=B'=-B'$ and $2\cdot C'=C'=-C'$. Thus part (iii) is also satisfied for the coloring $\{A,B,C\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the $|A|=1$ lemma applied in $G/H$ gives condition (iii).

nodes.name: Proof of the Lemma ($|A|=2$)
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:onecoset} we only have to show that one color is contained in a single coset of a proper subgroup $H<G$. We may assume that $A=\{0,a\}$. Let us show that $a$ generates a proper subgroup $H$ of $G$. Suppose on the contrary that the cyclic group generated by $a$ is the whole group $G=\langle a \rangle\cong \Z/n\Z$. Since $\{-a,a,3a\}$ can not be rainbow, we have $c(-a)=c(3a)$. Since $\{-3a,0,3a\}$ can not be rainbow we have $c(-3a)=c(3a)$. By iterating this argument, we have $$c(-a)=c(3a)=c(-3a)=c(5a)=c(-5a)= ... =c((n-2)a)=c(-(n-2)a),$$ so that the color class of $-a$ has $n-2$ elements. But then the third one is empty, a contradiction. Hence \textcolor{black}{$A\subset \langle a \rangle=H<G$} and, by Lemma~\ref{lem:onecoset}, \textcolor{black}{parts (i), (ii) and (iii) of} Theorem~\ref{thm:main} \textcolor{black}{are satisfied}.
nodes.statement_short: Show $a$ generates a proper subgroup: otherwise iterating the non-rainbow condition makes one color class have $n-2$ elements.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: Reduce to the one-coset lemma
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:onecoset} we only have to show that one color is contained in a single coset of a proper subgroup $H<G$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to place a color class in one coset of a proper subgroup.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: Assume $\langle a\rangle=G$ for contradiction
nodes.statement: We may assume that $A=\{0,a\}$. Let us show that $a$ generates a proper subgroup $H$ of $G$. Suppose on the contrary that the cyclic group generated by $a$ is the whole group $G=\langle a \rangle\cong \Z/n\Z$.
nodes.statement_short: Suppose instead that $a$ generates all of $G$.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: Iterate the non-rainbow condition
nodes.statement: Since $\{-a,a,3a\}$ can not be rainbow, we have $c(-a)=c(3a)$. Since $\{-3a,0,3a\}$ can not be rainbow we have $c(-3a)=c(3a)$. By iterating this argument, we have $$c(-a)=c(3a)=c(-3a)=c(5a)=c(-5a)= ... =c((n-2)a)=c(-(n-2)a),$$ so that the color class of $-a$ has $n-2$ elements. But then the third one is empty, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Chaining $c(-a)=c(3a)=\cdots$ makes one class have $n-2$ elements, emptying the third.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: Conclude via the one-coset lemma
nodes.statement: Hence \textcolor{black}{$A\subset \langle a \rangle=H<G$} and, by Lemma~\ref{lem:onecoset}, \textcolor{black}{parts (i), (ii) and (iii) of} Theorem~\ref{thm:main} \textcolor{black}{are satisfied}.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $A$ lies in the proper subgroup $\langle a\rangle$ and the previous lemma applies.

nodes.name: Proof of the Lemma ($|A|=|B|=3$, $|A+B|=6$)
nodes.statement: Let $A=\{0,a,a'\}$. It can be shown (see e.g. \cite{grynkiewicz}) that only two possibilities occur if $|A+B|=|A|+|B|=6$: either $B$ is a transllate of $A$ or one of the sets, say $A$, is an arithmetic progression, and the second one, $B$, is an arithmetic progression of length four with the same difference and with one element removed. Suppose that $B=A+x=\{ x,x+a,x+a'\}$ for some $x\in G$. Since $\{-x,0,x\}$ can not be rainbow we have $-x\in A\cup B$. If $-x\in A$ then $0\in A\cap B$, a contradiction. Thus $-x\in B$ and $a=-2x$. Since $\{0,x,2x\}$ can not be rainbow we have $2x\in A\cup B$. If $2x\in B$ then $x\in A\cap B$ (since $A=B-x$). Thus $2x=a$ which implies $B=\{ -x,x,3x\}$ and $A=\{-2x,0,2x\}$ and both sets are arithmetic progressions with the same difference contradicting $|A+B|=|A|+|B|$. Suppose now that $A$ is an arithmetic progression with difference $d$. If $A$ generates a proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ then the result follows from Lemma \ref{lem:onecoset}. Hence we may assume that $A=\{0,1,2\}$ and $G$ is the cyclic group of order $n$. Moreover $B=\{ x, x+2,x+3\}$ for some $x\in \Z/n\Z\setminus \{0,1,2,n-3,n-2,n-1\}$. If $\{0,x,-x\}$ is not rainbow, since $-x\in \{1,2\}$ \textcolor{black}{can not hold} and $n$ is odd, we must have $-x=x+3$. But then $x=(n-3)/2$ and $\{0,(n-1)/2, (n+1)/2\}$ is rainbow. \textcolor{black}{This contradiction completes the proof.}
nodes.statement_short: Grynkiewicz's classification leaves two configurations; each produces a rainbow triple, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: Two possible configurations
nodes.statement: Let $A=\{0,a,a'\}$. It can be shown (see e.g. \cite{grynkiewicz}) that only two possibilities occur if $|A+B|=|A|+|B|=6$: either $B$ is a transllate of $A$ or one of the sets, say $A$, is an arithmetic progression, and the second one, $B$, is an arithmetic progression of length four with the same difference and with one element removed.
nodes.statement_short: Cited structure theory: either $B$ is a translate of $A$, or both are (almost) progressions.

nodes.name: Case $B=A+x$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $B=A+x=\{ x,x+a,x+a'\}$ for some $x\in G$. Since $\{-x,0,x\}$ can not be rainbow we have $-x\in A\cup B$. If $-x\in A$ then $0\in A\cap B$, a contradiction. Thus $-x\in B$ and $a=-2x$. Since $\{0,x,2x\}$ can not be rainbow we have $2x\in A\cup B$. If $2x\in B$ then $x\in A\cap B$ (since $A=B-x$). Thus $2x=a$ which implies $B=\{ -x,x,3x\}$ and $A=\{-2x,0,2x\}$ and both sets are arithmetic progressions with the same difference contradicting $|A+B|=|A|+|B|$.
nodes.statement_short: The translate case forces both sets to be progressions with the same difference, contradiction.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: Case $A$ an arithmetic progression
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $A$ is an arithmetic progression with difference $d$. If $A$ generates a proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ then the result follows from Lemma \ref{lem:onecoset}. Hence we may assume that $A=\{0,1,2\}$ and $G$ is the cyclic group of order $n$. Moreover $B=\{ x, x+2,x+3\}$ for some $x\in \Z/n\Z\setminus \{0,1,2,n-3,n-2,n-1\}$. If $\{0,x,-x\}$ is not rainbow, since $-x\in \{1,2\}$ \textcolor{black}{can not hold} and $n$ is odd, we must have $-x=x+3$. But then $x=(n-3)/2$ and $\{0,(n-1)/2, (n+1)/2\}$ is rainbow. \textcolor{black}{This contradiction completes the proof.}
nodes.statement_short: In the progression case an explicit rainbow triple appears.
nodes.section: 4 Small color classes and color classes in arithmetic progresion

nodes.name: Proof of the Lemma (two classes are almost--progressions)
nodes.statement: If $d$ generates a proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ then $A$ is contained in a single coset of $H$ and the result follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:onecoset}. Thus we may assume that $d$ generates the full group, so that $G$ is the cyclic group $\Z/n\Z$ and we may assume $d=1$ \textcolor{black}{(since the property of being rainbow--free is invariant by dilations)}. We will show that in this case $c$ contains a rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progression. Let $b$ be the minimum circular distance from elements in $A$ to elements in $B$. If $b=1$ we may assume that $n-1\in A$ and $0\in B$. Since $\max\{ |A|,|B|\}\le (n-5)/2$ we have $(n-1)/2\in C$ giving the rainbow $\{ 0,(n-1)/2, n-1\}$. Suppose now that $b>1$. Since $|A|\ge 4$ we may assume that $\{n-1,0\}\subset A$ and $\{1,2,\ldots ,b'\}\subseteq C$ and $b'+1\in B$ for some $b'\ge b$. If $b'$ is odd then $\{0,(b'+1)/2,b'+1\}$ is rainbow and if $b'$ is even then $\{n-1, (b'+2)/2, b'+1\}$ is rainbow.
nodes.statement_short: If $d$ generates $G$, a circular-distance argument exhibits a rainbow triple; otherwise apply the one-coset lemma.

nodes.name: Case $d$ generates a proper subgroup
nodes.statement: If $d$ generates a proper subgroup $H$ of $G$ then $A$ is contained in a single coset of $H$ and the result follows by Lemma~\ref{lem:onecoset}.
nodes.statement_short: If $\langle d\rangle\ne G$ the one-coset lemma finishes.

nodes.name: Reduce to $G=\Z/n\Z$, $d=1$
nodes.statement: Thus we may assume that $d$ generates the full group, so that $G$ is the cyclic group $\Z/n\Z$ and we may assume $d=1$ \textcolor{black}{(since the property of being rainbow--free is invariant by dilations)}. We will show that in this case $c$ contains a rainbow $3$--term arithmetic progression.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise normalize to the cyclic group with difference $1$.

nodes.name: Introduce the minimum circular distance $b$
nodes.statement: Let $b$ be the minimum circular distance from elements in $A$ to elements in $B$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $b$, the minimal circular gap between $A$ and $B$.

nodes.name: Case $b=1$
nodes.statement: If $b=1$ we may assume that $n-1\in A$ and $0\in B$. Since $\max\{ |A|,|B|\}\le (n-5)/2$ we have $(n-1)/2\in C$ giving the rainbow $\{ 0,(n-1)/2, n-1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $b=1$ the midpoint $(n-1)/2$ lies in $C$, giving a rainbow triple.

nodes.name: Case $b>1$
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $b>1$. Since $|A|\ge 4$ we may assume that $\{n-1,0\}\subset A$ and $\{1,2,\ldots ,b'\}\subseteq C$ and $b'+1\in B$ for some $b'\ge b$. If $b'$ is odd then $\{0,(b'+1)/2,b'+1\}$ is rainbow and if $b'$ is even then $\{n-1, (b'+2)/2, b'+1\}$ is rainbow.
nodes.statement_short: For $b>1$ an explicit rainbow triple is produced in each parity case.
